# Republican Party efforts to disrupt the 2024 United States presidential election__disambig_1

}}
The '''Republican Party's efforts to disrupt the 2024 United States presidential election' include legislative, legal, and administrative strategies to affect voter access, election oversight, and post-election certification processes. They include tentatives to modify voting laws so as to restrict demographics more likely to vote Democrat, and a push to place partisan figures in Republican-led states in order to oversee the interpretation and the enforcement of election laws. These strategies have been promoted within certain Republican Party circles using alarmist claims about election integrity, many of which trace back to election denial movement in the United States.
Numerous court cases challenged aspects of the voting process and aimed to set precedents for handling election disputes. While proponents contend that these measures ensure election security, critics argue that that eroding public trust in election fairness and undermine the democratic process.
Background
Fraud grievances
For decades, Republicans sought evidence of what they allege is rampant electoral fraud; multiple studies found that electoral fraud is extremely rare. Heritage claimed having found more than 1,500 instances of fraud over 42 years; an analysis led by the Brennan Center for Justice found the claim "grossly exaggerated". In a 1980 speech, Paul Weyrich stated the reason to restrict voting: "our leverage in the elections quite candidly goes up as the voting populace goes down."
As president, Trump blamed his popular vote loss to millions of undocumented migrants. After his 2020 loss, Trump kept repeating that the election had been rigged, a baseless allegation that came to be known as his big lie. Trump established a commision in May 2017; it was disbanded months later, with Matthew Dunlap writing Mike Pence and Kris Kobach that the commission found nothing substantial. The commission did not find a single instance of a noncitizen voting. Critics said the commission intended to disenfranchise or deter legal voters. Kobach had a history of making false or unsubstantiated allegations of voting fraud to advocate for voting restrictions.
A movement emerged to advance this narrative. Media such as Fox News, Newsmax, and OANN promoted fraud allegations in the weeks following the 2020 election, including conspiracy theories that voting machines had been rigged. In response, Dominion and Smartmatic filed defamation lawsuits; Fox News agreed to settle for $787.5 million after it was revealed that top on-air personalities and executives knew the allegations were false but continued to promote them anyway. In 2000 Mules'', Dinesh D'Souza accused Democratic Party operatives of ballot collecting across five swing states during the 2020 election; he apologized for his lies in 2024.
By April, 2024, dozens of Republicans in four states have been indicted for their involvement in promoting conspiracies, such as the fake electors or the Pence card plots. Those indicted included Trump and Christina Bobb, who led the Republican National Committee election integrity legal efforts in the 2024 presidential election. In September, Hanna Rosin described how January 6 insurrectionists have created "a new mythology on the right". The Justice Department planned to monitor compliance with voting rights laws on Election Day in 27 states.
Voting purges
Since at least 2003, journalists, election security experts, and activists have repeatedly warned about security vulnerabilities and other flaws in the election infrastructure of the United States.
Commentators have repeatedly accused the Republican Party of applying deceptive methods in order to win elections. The New Republic alleged that Republican Party political campaigns have a history of applying "voter intimidation techniques, more direct threats of violence, foreign disinformation, and super PAC and dark money skullduggery" as strategies, citing:
* the possible sabotage of Vietnam War peace talks during the 1968 election;
* the Watergate scandal during the 1972 election;
* the 1980 October Surprise theory;
* the tactics of Lee Atwater during the 1988 election;
* the "butterfly ballots"
* actions of Katherine Harris
* Brooks Brothers riot
* Bush v. Gore
* the 2002 New Hampshire Senate election phone jamming scandal
* and the swiftboating of John Kerry during the 2004 election.
Truthout cited the Volusia error during the 2000 election; voter roll purges during the 2000 and 2004 elections (in Florida and Ohio, respectively); false information about voting logistics by election boards controlled by Republicans; voter intimidation; and voter ID laws. Truthout also cited "voter irregularities" in Ohio during the 2004 election involving a Republican-connected company SMARTech, and also noted that Anonymous claimed without evidence that Karl Rove unsuccessfully attempted to use Mitt Romney's ORCA get-out-the-vote system to rig the 2012 election in Ohio in a similar fashion as alleged to have occurred in 2004.
In Al Jazeera America, Greg Palast warned in 2014 of the impact that the Interstate Voter Registration Crosscheck Program, which he accused of overrepresenting Black, Asian and Hispanic voters in its efforts to purge potentially millions of names from voter rolls, could have on the 2014 and 2016 elections. Palast assessed that 1.1 million voters were removed from voter rolls by the 2016 election, while the Brennan Center determined that nearly 16 million voters were removed by states between 2014 and 2016. Crosscheck had been criticized by journalists and researchers for poor accuracy.
Following Trump's 2020 loss amid his false allegations of fraud, Republican lawmakers initiated a sweeping effort to make voting laws more restrictive in several states across the country and to take control of the administrative management of elections at the state and local level. By 2023, organizations funded by dark money had met quietly with officials in Republican-controlled states to create an incubator of policies that would restrict ballot access and amplify false claims that fraud is rampant in elections. Led by the Heritage Foundation, the groups include the Honest Elections Project, which is among a network of conservative organizations associated with Leonard Leo, a longtime prominent figure in the Federalist Society.
Russian connections
Craig Unger documented ties between the Republican Party and the Russian government dating back to at least 1997, including Tom DeLay visiting Moscow to meet Viktor Chernomyrdin, Ed Buckham's U.S. Family Network being funded $1 million by Russians to influence DeLay's vote on bailing out the Russian economy, and Paul Manafort's ties to Russia (among others). Manafort had given polling data to a Russian intelligence officer in 2016. The Washington Spectator traced these ties back to a 1995 visit to Russia by Allan C. Carlson, who subsequently formed the World Congress of Families after observing commonalities between American and Russian conservatives. Nafeez Ahmed has also noted the ties between the Heritage and the Danube Institute, which is funded by the government of Viktor Orbán and is supportive of the Russian government. Paul Dans, the former leader of Project 2025, appeared on a podcast from Tenet Media, which was accused by the Department of Justice of being operated by Russian agents.
The Wall Street Journal reported in October 2024 that Musk had been in regular contact with Vladimir Putin, Sergey Kiriyenko, and other high ranking Russian government officials since late 2022, discussing personal topics, business and geopolitical matters. On November 15, Democratic senators Jack Reed and Jeanne Shaheen asked the Pentagon and Department of Justice to investigate these contacts, citing national security concerns. Musk has a security clearance with the United States federal government, and several federal agencies such as the Pentagon, the Space Force and NASA depend on technology from Musk's company SpaceX.
Tom Nichols theorized that the Republican Party's overall affinity for Russia and Vladimir Putin in particular may be due in part to questions about the party's long-term viability which could be addressed by "nationalist appeals, combined with electoral fraud and selective use of the prison system" that were modeled by Putin.
International Democracy Union
The Republican Party is a member of the International Democracy Union (IDU), which The Tyee described as a global group that is "dedicated to electing right-wing governments around the world". Under the leadership of Stephen Harper, Mike Roman was the treasurer and then assistant chairman of the IDU until Roman was indicted for allegedly participating in attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election. During the 2008 United States presidential election, Roman had shared a video of the New Black Panther Party voter intimidation case, which Richard Hasen had alleged to be an example of a false or exaggerated claim of voter fraud. Roman had written in a 2008 blog post, "If an election is worth winning, then there is someone willing to steal it."
Voting machines
At an August 2021 event organized by Mike Lindell, copies of software from Dominion Voting Systems equipment in Colorado and Michigan were distributed and posted to the public Internet. Election security experts warned that the release undermines trust in election security and allows for hackers to conduct vulnerability assessments, counter defenses, "sabotage the system, alter ballot design or even try to change results". Three vendors dominate election technology in the United States, limiting the ability for election officials to replace an existing system. Mike Lindell stated that his goal is to remove voting machines entirely and switch to paper ballots, a process that election officials warned would be tedious, time-consuming and prone to errors.
CNN reported that in text messages to Doug Logan, the CEO of Cyber Ninjas, which conducted the 2021 Maricopa County presidential ballot audit, Michael Flynn expressed a goal to "fundamentally change the way votes are counted at the state level".
In August 2023, Matthew DePerno, the former Republican nominee for the 2022 Michigan Attorney General election, and former Republican state representative Daire Rendon were charged with "undue possession of a voting machine, willfully damaging a voting machine and conspiracy". DePerno spread false claims about the 2020 United States presidential election.
Election denial activists had spread a password that they alleged to be used in Dominion voting machines in Georgia, including wearing the alleged password on t-shirts.
In 2020, J. Alex Halderman, a computer science and engineering professor, discovered a software vulnerability in Georgia's voting machines which made it possible for hackers to change votes. While Dominion developed a patch to address these vulnerabilities, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said that the machines would be updated after the 2024 election, dismissing Halderman's findings as "theoretical and imaginary."
In December 2022, election experts sent a letter to the United States Department of Justice that described a "multi-state conspiracy to copy voting software" that was at least partially funded by notable Trump supporters such as Sidney Powell and asking for a federal investigation. In December 2023, a follow-up open letter from computer scientists, election security experts and voter advocacy organizations listed repeated attempts by allies of Donald Trump to access voting system software in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Nevada and Colorado, again calling for a federal investigation, noting that the software is used nationwide. Entire election databases from multiple counties were also copied. Electronic pollbooks, ballot scanners, servers for vote counting, USB flash drives, and memory cards were also copied in Coffee County, Georgia. At least one breach had also occurred in North Carolina. In at least four cases, election officials had to decertify or replace voting equipment. Voting experts expressed alarm over the breaches due to their breaking of the chain of custody over ballots and tabulators; as well as invasion of voter privacy. On November 13, 2024, a third open letter was sent by the same organization, Free Speech for People, to Kamala Harris, warning her of "serious election security breaches that have threatened the security and integrity of the 2024 elections" and urging her to request hand recounts in at least four swing states. The letter noted that voting system breaches have allowed for access to main servers, tabulators and election databases for both Dominion Voting Systems and Election Systems & Software, election vendors which collectively count approximately 70% of votes across the United States.
SMART Elections (a nonpartisan election integrity advocacy group that includes academics and activists) noted that Pro V&V, a voting system test laboratory, had approved software and hardware updates for Dominion and Election Systems & Software voting systems between March and September 2024, categorizing those updates as de minimis, which do not require testing. SMART Elections warned that this lack of testing for what it described as comprehensive updates risked malware entering the voting systems. SMART Elections stated that, since at least July 2024, the website for Pro V&V had error messages, and by February 2025, the site had been nonfunctional. Newsweek reported in June 2025 that Jack Cobb, the director of Pro V&V, had denied these allegations.
Free Speech for People, a left-leaning nonprofit advocacy group for election and campaign finance reform, published three open letters between 2022 and 2024 to the United States Department of Justice, Federal Bureau of Investigation, U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and Kamala Harris, urging either a federal investigation (pre-election) or a hand recount (post-election).
Funding
The National Committee for Responsive Philanthropy and The American Prospect reported that, between 2020 and 2022, over 3,500 foundations and high net-worth donors provided over $1 billion to about 150 nonprofit organizations that supported voter suppression activities. Donors included the Bradley Foundation, Searle Freedom Trust, Sarah Scaife Foundation, and the Charles Koch Foundation. Public charities with donor-advised funds (DAF) that also provided funding include DonorsTrust, Fidelity Charitable, Goldman Sachs, National Philanthropic Trust, and Schwab Charitable. The specific donors to these DAFs are unknown as of March 2025.
Other known funders of the above activities include the Uihlein family, Mike Lindell, Sidney Powell, Rebecca Dunn, Robert Beadles, the Conservative Partnership Institute, The 85 Fund, Concord Fund, Ziklag, and Elon Musk.
America PAC
Elon Musk contributed at least $260 million to efforts to re-elect Trump, including through three super PACs (America PAC, RBG PAC, and the MAHA Alliance). Steve Bannon had credited Musk financing Trump's campaign as "the reason we won." During the election campaign, Musk had established a "war room" in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, believing that the state was crucial for Trump to win the election. Musk had promoted Trump's campaign to his (Musk's) followers on X/Twitter, and had spread unfounded conspiracy theories about the Democratic Party. X had colluded with the Trump campaign to block links to a dossier of JD Vance, suspending the account of the journalist who published the dossier. Musk had repeatedly shared deepfake media of Kamala Harris, including with the use of Grok-2, a text-to-image model created by xAI. He has claimed without evidence that, if Trump did not win, the 2024 election would be the last in the United States.
America PAC had posted digital ads asking viewers to register to vote, but viewers in swing states were asked to submit their address, cell phone number and age, without directing them to a voter registration page. The PAC's privacy policy allows it to use this data for "other [political] activities and/or fundraising campaigns" such as door-to-door canvassing. As a result, the Michigan Secretary of State's Office and the North Carolina Board of Elections have opened investigations into the PAC in August 2024, while the North Carolina Attorney General's Office started to informally review the PAC. As of October 2024, Michigan had not found evidence of the PAC violating state campaign finance law.
At least 18 Pennsylvania residents – mostly registered Democrats - have received checks from America PAC Petition despite not having signed the petition or no knowledge of family members or friends who signed them up. The petition's stated goal was to sign up 1 million registered voters in swing states to show support for the First and Second Amendments, giving away $1 million to one petition signee every day until Election Day (in addition to $100 per petition referral), and had asked for their full names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses. Voter registration data in Pennsylvania – which includes names, addresses, registration status, and political affiliation – can be purchased from the Pennsylvania State Department for $20. While America PAC stated that it would verify the information of the check recipients for accuracy, many of these recipients stated that no verification process had occurred. As of December 2024, about 20 complaints have been sent to the Pennsylvania Attorney General Office's Bureau of Consumer Protection. The majority of petitioners who were selected as winners of the $1 million sweepstakes were from Pennsylvania. One of the sweepstakes winners had worked on the Trump campaign between June and October 2024. Another sweepstakes winner had the same name and lived in the same town as a person who ran for county supervisor in 2022.
On Election Day 2024, Musk stated that he planned for America PAC to be involved in the 2026 United States midterm elections, "any intermediate elections, as well as ... elections at the district attorney level." Larry Krasner, the Philadelphia district attorney, had filed a lawsuit against Musk and America PAC a week prior on October 28 over the PAC's $1 million giveaway scheme.
Over 1 million people in seven swing states had signed up with the petition, with Krasner arguing that they were "scammed for their information." On November 4, a judge dismissed the lawsuit, arguing that Krasner "failed to provide any evidence of misuse beyond mere speculation."
Legal support
Known lawyers and law firms supporting the above activities, some of whom were involved in the attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election, include the "election integrity unit" of the Republican National Committee, Jones Day, Consovoy McCarthy, Dhillon Law Group Inc., Cleta Mitchell, Bruce Castor, Michael van der Veen, Christina Bobb, Public Interest Legal Foundation, America First Legal, Alan Dershowitz, and Kurt Olsen.
Election vigilantes
The Election Integrity Act of 2021 in Georgia (SB 202) allows persons to file an unlimited number of challenges to voter registrations in the state. As of November 2022, at least 149,168 challenges have been filed, primarily against young or Black voters, and no charges of voter fraud have been made. These lists of challenges have been created by True the Vote, which claimed to partially obtain them from the National Change of Address registry. Brad Raffensperger stated that "though federal law restricts our ability to update our voter registration lists, the Elector Challenge is a vehicle under our law to ensure voter integrity." Bee Nguyen accused the law of bypassing the National Voter Registration Act of 1993, which forbids voter registration purges 90 days prior to an election. SB 202 in turn potentially violates that federal law as well as the Civil Rights Act and Ku Klux Klan Act.
Republican elections activist Cleta Mitchell said "the only way [Democrats] win is to cheat". She was a key figure in Trump's attempts to overturn the 2020 election results, participating in the January 2021 Trump–Raffensperger phone call that attempted to change the certified 2020 presidential election results in Georgia. That year, in association with the RNC, she launched the Election Integrity Network (EIN) to recruit, train and deploy election deniers as poll workers in eight key states for the 2024 presidential election. In recordings of spring 2022 organizing meetings obtained by Politico, RNC National Election Integrity director Josh Findlay, referencing EIN, was heard to tell others that the RNC would support efforts to provide staff, organization, and "muscle" in key states. The New York Times reported that the EIN "has done more than any other group to take Mr. Trump's falsehoods about corruption in the democratic system and turn them into action". Gaining access to over 400 hours of Zoom meetings, The New York Times reported that EIN had closely coordinated with the RNC, four Republican secretaries of state, and a dozen state legislatures. The group was funded by multiple Republican megadonors associated with Trump, and had successfully spread conspiracy theories about voting with several right-wing media outlets and had installed activists on election boards and thousands as poll monitors and workers. EIN has also been collaborating with other groups to challenge voter rolls, including VoteRef (run by Gina Swoboda and funded by Restoration PAC, a Super PAC predominantly funded by Richard Uihlein) and Check My Vote. EIN has also been collaborating with the Election Transparency Initiative, headed by Ken Cuccinelli. The Pennsylvania Department of State described these voter registration challenges as "an attempt to circumvent the list maintenance processes that are carefully prescribed by state and federal law," which would result in "disenfranchisement, unnecessary litigation, and a harassing diversion of already-stretched county resources."
Elon Musk
Academic researchers had found that, shortly after Musk tweeted his endorsement of Trump in July 2024, Musk's X/Twitter account had received a strong and sustained increase in engagement compared to other high-profile political accounts; and that right-wing accounts had higher post visibility compared to left-wing accounts during the same time period. An analysis from the Washington Post also found that, between July 2023 and October 2024, tweets from Republican politicians had significantly more virality compared to those from Democrats.
In July 2024, Jerry Nadler wrote a letter to the House Judiciary Committee asking for an investigation into whether X/Twitter had limited users from following Kamala Harris' official presidential campaign account, with Nadler and NBC News noting that at least 16 accounts had posted that they were unable to follow the account.
Shortly after the attempted assassination of Donald Trump in Florida in September 2024, Musk published and then deleted a tweet stating that "no one is even trying to assassinate" President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris.
Musk had funded the dark money network Building America's Future since 2022, and has also given money to Citizens for Sanity through that network. Building America's Future also funded the Fair Election Fund, a group tied to Musk adviser Phil Cox and supporters of Ron DeSantis' presidential campaign, which paid $75,000 in bounties for alleged election fraud claims and promised to publicize them, but did not as of February 2025. That group had also posted ads that attacked North Carolina State Board of Elections officials that delayed adding Cornel West and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on the state ballot. The group's spokesperson was Doug Collins.
During town hall events in Pennsylvania in October, Musk spread false conspiracy theories about voting machines, linking voting machines from Dominion to election losses for the Republican Party. He advocated for elections to be run with only hand-counted paper ballots, stating "I'm a technologist, I know a lot about computers. And I'm like, the last thing I would do is trust a computer program, because it's just too easy to hack." He further advocated for only in-person voting with identification, despite America PAC supporting mail-in voting and absentee ballots.
During the 2024 election, X (formerly Twitter) released "Election Integrity Community", a social media feed run by America PAC that promotes posts that are alleged to support claims by users of voter fraud, "regardless of their accuracy." X/Twitter under Musk had previously softened its civic integrity policy, laying off trust and safety staff, including those who had handled election policy, platform manipulation and disinformation. Claims of election fraud had spread on X/Twitter with little moderation. The Center for Countering Digital Hate reported in November 2024 that false or misleading claims about the election had 2 billion views on X/Twitter in 2024 (promoted by Musk himself in at least 87 posts).
At a rally in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania on November 5, 2024, Donald Trump stated: "[Musk] really is watching this whole voting process. ... He looked at some that were just shipped in, some of these vote-counting computers. He knew it before it even came in the door. He looked like at the back of it, 'Oh, I know that one.' He knows this stuff better than anyone."
PopCrush reported that on the same day, during an interview with Tucker Carlson, Musk asked his son if they should help Trump win the election, to which he (his son) agreed. His son then said, "We're in SpaceX and we quietly do just whatever we want".
On his podcast shortly after Election Day, Joe Rogan told Theo Von that Musk had "created an app" to know what the election results were four hours in advance. , how the app worked and what data it used are unknown.
The day after the election, an election official in the Tulare County, California Elections Office stated that the office used Starlink, which improved "access to connectivity". A few days later, another official stated that Starlink was only used to connect office laptops to the Internet to access their election database, solely for the purpose of checking in voters or verifying their registration status. Verified Voting confirmed that Starlink was used in several jurisdictions for electronic pollbooks during the election, but that it was not involved in counting votes. AFP reported that most, if not all, ballot marking devices and vote tabulators are not connected to the Internet, and that Starlink had been used in elections since at least 2022 without controversy.
At a Turning Point USA conference in December 2024, Ken Paxton claimed that during a meeting on November 3, 2024 (two days before Election Day), Elon Musk told him that he was "now involved in every battleground state, and we're going to win every battleground state." During the conference, Paxton said that he was "convinced that whatever rocket science thing [Musk] did made a huge difference in this election".
During Donald Trump's pre-inauguration rally on January 19, 2025, Trump credited Musk for his contributions to the campaign in Pennsylvania, stating "[Musk] knows those computers better than anybody. All those computers. Those vote-counting computers. And we ended up winning Pennsylvania like in a landslide." Democratic congresswoman Jasmine Crockett questioned whether Trump had admitted that he and Musk had committed electoral fraud, while Newsweek reported that Dan Goldman urged an investigation.
During a meeting with state governors on February 21, 2025, Trump stated: "If that were a close election, you'd have to wait for weeks and weeks and weeks. You've got to finish fast, Brian [Kemp]. Thank you for your help. We did very well in Georgia. It was very nice." He also said, "I did ask Elon [Musk] because he knows more about computers than anybody, and I said, 'What do you think of the voting system?' He said, 'Computers are not meant for voting. It's just not a good, it's too many transactions taking place too quickly. It's just not', he said".
On the same day, People reported that Ashley St. Clair filed court petitions against Musk for full custody of her son and for Musk to be acknowledged as the father. In a 2024 text message exchange submitted as part of the filings, Musk said regarding death threats to himself: "The threat level will reach insane levels until the election is decided" and that "loose lips sink ships".
During a March 2025 interview with Musk on Ted Cruz's podcast, Cruz recalled that, during September or October 2024, Musk told him, "I don't want a job in Washington. All I want is the login for every computer." Cruz said that this request "sounded kind of weird". Musk claimed, in the context of his actions with the Department of Government Efficiency, that "the government is run by computers" and that "the only way to reconcile the databases and get rid of waste and fraud is to actually look at the computers and see what's going on."
In April 2025, X/Twitter sued Minnesota attorney general Keith Ellison over a 2023 state law banning online posts of deepfakes that spread misinformation within 90 days of an election with the intent to influence that election or harm a political candidate, with X/Twitter claiming free speech violations.
